hook: A farm store sells two rat poisons in nearly identical bags. One label says DANGER and the other says CAUTION. The difference comes from one number measured in the lab: how many milligrams of each product, per kilogram of animal, it takes to kill half of a test group. That number is the LD50, and a smaller one means a more dangerous chemical.

prereq.q: A substance builds up in one fish over its lifetime because the fish takes it in faster than it gets rid of it. What is this called?
prereq.why: Buildup inside one organism over time is bioaccumulation; biomagnification is the rise in concentration up a food chain.

prereq.q: How many milligrams are in 2.5 grams?
prereq.why: There are 1,000 mg in a gram: $2.5\,\text{g} \times \frac{1{,}000\,\text{mg}}{1\,\text{g}} = 2{,}500\,\text{mg}$.

figure.caption: Test rats killed at each dose of a pesticide (invented data). Go across from 50% to the line, then down: the LD50 is 40 mg/kg.

chain.cause: Researchers give groups of test animals larger and larger doses (mg per kg of body mass)
chain.effect: a larger percent of each group dies

chain.cause: They plot percent killed against dose and read across from 50%
chain.effect: the dose under that point is the LD50

chain.cause: A substance with a lower LD50 kills half the animals at a smaller dose
chain.effect: it is more toxic and gets a stronger warning label

chain.cause: Multiplying the LD50 by a body mass, with kilograms cancelling
chain.effect: gives the whole-body dose in milligrams for an animal of that size

ideas: Toxicity is how harmful a substance is. The dose is how much enters the body, usually in milligrams per kilogram of body mass (mg/kg).
LD50 is the dose that kills 50% of a test population. A lower LD50 means a more toxic substance.
Whole-body dose: $\text{LD}_{50} \times \text{body mass}$, for example $40\,\frac{\text{mg}}{\text{kg}} \times 0.25\,\text{kg} = 10\,\text{mg}$. Write the units so kilograms visibly cancel.
LD50s come from animal tests, so they only estimate the effect on people, and they say nothing about harm that does not kill.

misconception.wrong: A chemical with an LD50 of 5,000 mg/kg is more toxic than one with an LD50 of 5 mg/kg, because 5,000 is bigger.
misconception.right: It is the reverse. The LD50 is the dose needed to kill half the animals, so the chemical that needs only 5 mg/kg is 1,000 times as toxic.

summary: LD50 is the dose, in milligrams per kilogram of body mass, that kills half of a test population; it is read off a graph of percent killed against dose at the 50% line. The lower the LD50, the more toxic the substance. Multiply the LD50 by a body mass to get a whole-body dose, writing the units so kilograms cancel, and convert milligrams to grams when asked.
